_comment: Half the Town. Seven stops round the old centre of Castres, written for a Monday evening when the museums are shut. Everything is outdoors. The town is flat: the walk runs 181 m down to 171 m at the river, 901 m in all, and climbs three metres it had already climbed. The first walk written under contract.voice = plain, so every stop, question and hint is held to the shorter caps and the ban on essay voice. Four questions, three location gates, one drinks stop on the quay. Every coordinate, street, shop and bar named here came out of data/osm/castres.json and data/elevation/castres.json. Each answer is readable on the spot: a street plaque, the name on a cathedral, a memorial, a river sign.
name: Half the Town
tagline: a walk round a town that split in two

intro.lead: Seven stops round the old centre of Castres.
intro.body:
Just under a kilometre, about an hour. It is flat.

Four stops ask a question you can only answer by looking. Three just need you standing in the right place.

Built for a Monday evening. Everything is outdoors and free. The museums are shut. The shops and bars in the centre are not.
intro.start: Start on Place de la République, by the theatre. Leave the square on its north west side and walk forty metres along the narrow street.

topics.name: Two Churches and a Court
topics.blurb: Half the town was Protestant. The king gave it a court of its own to keep the peace.

topics.name: Two Men From Here
topics.blurb: A mathematician who judged cases by day. A politician shot for arguing against a war.

topics.name: The River and the Fountain
topics.blurb: The town made leather and cloth on the water. Nobody could drink it.

outro:
That is the seven.

The bars on the quay are behind you. Les Arcades and S&L are both on Quai Tourcaudière.

If you want more, the Musée Goya is in the old bishop's palace by Place de la République. The formal garden behind it is open in the day.

stops.title: Where the Court Sat
stops.where: the narrow street off the north west corner of Place de la République
stops.look:
An ordinary back street with an odd name.

A court sat in Castres for most of a century. This street still carries its name.

The plaque is on the wall where the street meets the square.
stops.after:
The Chambre de l'Édit. The Edict of Nantes gave French Protestants courts of their own, with Catholic and Protestant judges in equal numbers.

Castres got one because half the town was Protestant.

It sat until 1679. Then the king moved it to Castelnaudary, and six years later he cancelled the Edict.
stops.after_spoken:
The Chambre de l'Édit. The Edict of Nantes gave French Protestants courts of their own, with Catholic and Protestant judges in equal numbers.

Castres got one because half the town was Protestant.

It sat until sixteen seventy nine. Then the king moved it to Castelnaudary, and six years later he cancelled the Edict.

stops.title: The Cathedral
stops.where: the cathedral, in the middle of the old town
stops.directions: From Rue Chambre de l'Édit, head east into the old town. About two hundred and fifty metres.

question.ask: The cathedral is named after a saint. Which one?
question.hint: It is on the front of the building and on the street sign beside it.

stops.look:
Big, plain and late. Work started in 1677.

There was an abbey on this spot for eight hundred years before that, and the monks lived by one man's rule. The church carries his name.
stops.after:
Benoît. Benedict, in English.

The abbey here was Benedictine and it came first. Castres exists because monks settled on the river in the ninth century.

By the time this church went up, the town had been arguing about religion for a hundred years. It is the Catholic half of that argument. You will see the other half later.

stops.title: The Fountain
stops.where: the fountain at the west end of Place Jean Jaurès
stops.directions: From the cathedral, head north through the lanes towards the main square. About a hundred and seventy metres.

question.ask: The fountain is named after the figures on it. What are they?
question.hint: There are several of them, in stone, and they are not adults.

stops.look:
A town on a river still needed a fountain. There were tanneries and dye works upstream.

Look at the stone figures on this one.
stops.after:
Cherubs. Angelots in French, and the fountain takes its name from them.

Castres drank from fountains like this until the town was plumbed. The river ran the trades and put something in the water at every one of them.

The square is the old corn market.
stops.directions_target: a stone fountain with cherubs on it, at the west end of Place Jean Jaurès

stops.title: The Mathematician
stops.where: the east end of Place Jean Jaurès
stops.directions:
From the fountain, go back to Rue Henri IV and walk the length of Place Jean Jaurès, which runs east. About a hundred metres.

Stop near the far end, where the square opens onto the quay.

gate.prompt: Stand at the east end of the square.

nudge.prompt: There is a small metal plaque to him set back off the north side of the square, in among the jewellers. It is easy to miss.

stops.look:
One of the great mathematicians of the sixteen hundreds lived and died in Castres.

He was a lawyer by trade. He did his sums in the evenings and published almost none of them.
stops.after:
Pierre de Fermat. He was a judge on the court in the street you started on, and he was buried here on 13 January 1665.

He wrote in the margins of his books. One note claimed a proof that a certain sum has no whole number answers. The margin, he said, was too small to hold it.

It took until the 1990s to find one.
stops.after_spoken:
Pierre de Fermat. He was a judge on the court in the street you started on, and he was buried here on the thirteenth of January sixteen sixty five.

He wrote in the margins of his books. One note claimed a proof that a certain sum has no whole number answers. The margin, he said, was too small to hold it.

It took until the nineteen nineties to find one.

stops.title: A Drink on the Quay
stops.where: the arcades on Quai Tourcaudière, by the statue
stops.directions:
From the east end of Place Jean Jaurès, turn onto Quai Tourcaudière, which runs north. About fifty metres.

Les Arcades is under the arches, a few doors along.

gate.prompt: Stand under the arcades, by the statue.

stops.look:
This is the stop for a drink. Etienne Coffee is next door if the bar is shut.

The statue is Jean Jaurès. He was born in Castres in 1859, and almost every town in France has a street named after him.
stops.after:
Jaurès taught philosophy, went into politics and became the leading French socialist of his day.

He spent the summer of 1914 arguing against the war that was coming. On 31 July a nationalist shot him through a café window in Paris.

France was at war three days later.
stops.after_spoken:
Jaurès taught philosophy, went into politics and became the leading French socialist of his day.

He spent the summer of nineteen fourteen arguing against the war that was coming. On the thirty first of July a nationalist shot him through a café window in Paris.

France was at war three days later.

stops.title: The Temple
stops.where: the Grand temple, on Rue du Consulat
stops.directions: From the arcades, head north through the lanes behind the square. About two hundred and twenty metres.
stops.look:
This is a Protestant temple. Look at the name. There is no saint in it.

Castres was one of the strongest Protestant towns in the south of France. The court you started at existed because of towns like this one.
stops.after:
This building is much younger than the argument.

When the Edict was cancelled in 1685, Protestant worship became illegal and the temples came down. Castres kept its Protestants anyway. They met in barns and in the woods for a hundred years.

Freedom came back with the Revolution, and buildings like this one followed.
stops.after_spoken:
This building is much younger than the argument.

When the Edict was cancelled in sixteen eighty five, Protestant worship became illegal and the temples came down. Castres kept its Protestants anyway. They met in barns and in the woods for a hundred years.

Freedom came back with the Revolution, and buildings like this one followed.
stops.directions_target: the Grand temple, on Rue du Consulat

stops.title: The Old Bridge
stops.where: the middle of the Pont Vieux
stops.directions: From the temple, head south east to the river. About a hundred and forty metres.

question.hint: There is a sign on the bridge or on the quay. Five letters.

stops.look:
Stop in the middle. The houses on the far bank are built out over the water.

The bottom of each one was a workshop. Tanners and dyers needed running water, and they needed a lot of it.
stops.after:
The Agout. Castres made leather and cloth for six hundred years and all of it needed this water.

The houses were workshops downstairs and homes upstairs. The waste went into the river, so the fountain on the square is where people drank.

The bridge under you is the oldest crossing in the town.
stops.directions_target: the Pont Vieux, with houses built out over the water on the far bank
